items.name: Agent-Reach
items.description: MIT-licensed Python CLI (v1.5.0, 6.4k forks, 374 commits, last commit 2026-09-16) that installs, health-checks and routes to upstream tools so an agent can read and search the internet: web via Jina Reader, YouTube captions via yt-dlp, RSS, GitHub via gh, Exa semantic search via MCP, plus Twitter/X, Reddit, Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and China-focused channels (Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, Xueqiu stocks, V2EX, Boss, Xiaoyuzhou podcasts). It is a glue layer, not a wrapper: after install the agent calls the upstream tools directly. Each platform has an ordered list of backends (first that really works wins) and `agent-reach doctor` reports which is live and how to fix the rest. Ships a SKILL.md with per-category reference files. Install is 'paste this URL to your agent'; default mode is read-only check, system changes need --system.
items.verdictNote: Mostly already covered. Do NOT install for web, YouTube, RSS, GitHub or search (you have Jina, Exa, Tavily, Firecrawl, Crawl4AI, SearXNG, Playwright, YouTube transcript MCP). Keep as an optional add-on for ONE gap: read-only Reddit and X research for finance-education and sports analytics, on a throwaway account, on an 8 GB GPU only. Steal its patterns now.
items.why: Ordered backends per capability, chosen by a REAL probe (does it actually return data), not just 'is the command installed'. Apply to the model router and to every data source in the swarm A `doctor` command that says which route is live and how to fix the rest. You should have one for the whole stack (local models, cloud models, database, automation) Safe-by-default installer: read-only check first, `--dry-run` preview, explicit flag for system changes, clean `uninstall` that removes stored credentials Credentials: stored in one file with 600 permissions, scrubbed from output, extracted from a browser one platform at a time (least privilege) Tests outnumber source: 606 pass, about 10.5k lines of tests for 7.3k lines of code; ruff and mypy both clean. A model for the Claude Code handoff standards URL guard written as 'public addresses only' using the standard library's is_global idea, covering odd IPv4 spellings. SEE : your own guard misses IPv6 and carrier-grade-NAT addresses Prompt-injection-aware install guide: explicit DO NOT list (no sudo, no system files, nothing inside the workspace) and fixed directories

warnings: ACCOUNT RISK: the X, Reddit, Instagram and Facebook routes use logged-in browser sessions or cookies, which breaks those platforms' terms. The author's own README says to use a throwaway account. Never connect your main brand accounts (Instagram, TikTok, etc.): a ban would hit your revenue brand
READ-ONLY ONLY: do not let any agent post, follow or message through these routes. That is the line between research and account-ban or spam territory
Third parties see the queries: Jina Reader receives every URL you read, Exa receives every search through its free MCP endpoint (free-tier limits and terms not verified)

'Paste this URL to your agent' installs from the moving `main` branch (pipx install of main.zip) with no pinned version. Treat install docs fetched by an agent as untrusted: pin a release tag and read the guide yourself first
Most channels target Chinese platforms (Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, Xueqiu, V2EX, Boss, Xiaoyuzhou) and are irrelevant to you unless you cover Chinese markets
Reddit has no zero-config route (anonymous access is blocked); it needs OpenCLI plus a desktop Chrome login, so it cannot run on the Windows server that hosts trading software
README includes sponsor ads and the author sells agent consulting; neither is a red flag, but 75k stars and a Trendshift badge are popularity, not an audit
One of 607 tests fails here only because this sandbox has GITHUB_TOKEN set; the test does not isolate the environment. Not a code bug

Platforms change anti-bot rules constantly; the project documents Bilibili blocking yt-dlp in June 2026 and a March 2026 wave of abandoned single-platform CLIs. Expect routes to break and rely on doctor
NOT RUN end to end: the sandbox cannot reach these platforms, so I verified code, tests and docs, not live scraping results

items.name: image-blaster
items.description: Claude Code skill pack (8 skills, 6 forked sub-agents, ~4,100 lines of Node scripts, no Python) that turns one image into: (1) GLB/OBJ meshes of each loose object via fal Hunyuan3D v3 (Meshy v6 optional), (2) a Gaussian-splat (.spz) of the empty static room plus a collider mesh via World Labs Marble 1.1, (3) ambient loop and per-object impact SFX via ElevenLabs on fal. Includes a React/three.js/Spark/Rapier viewer with a walkable character. Pipeline: analyse image -> list liftable objects (human confirms) -> remove them from the photo to make a clean plate -> generate world from the plate, generate each object from its own isolated reference image, generate SFX. The object step also works alone on any single image, without World Labs.
items.verdictNote: ADD as an optional pay-per-use specialist tool. Use the object-to-mesh step and the SFX step now (cheap, no World Labs dependency); HOLD the World Labs step until the AMD deal and API commercial terms are clear. Run a pilot with a hard fal spend cap only after the indie web-game 2D/3D question is answered. Copy its patterns into your own skills regardless.
items.why: FILLS A GAP, replaces nothing: you had no hosted image-to-mesh tool. Free local alternative is Trellis2 via ComfyUI, but it shares the 8 GB card with Flux and VoiceStudio NOT RUN: no API keys and the sandbox cannot reach the providers, so mesh and world quality are the README's claims, not the result. Pilot before relying on it WORLD LABS RISK: AMD announced an $8.2B all-stock acquisition on 2026-09-28 (AMD newsroom, Bloomberg, CNBC; close expected end of 2026). Neither side has committed to Marble API pricing or continuity, and the Terms already allow suspension and assignment. Do not build a revenue path on the World API yet WORLD LABS COMMERCIAL RIGHTS UNVERIFIED: docs name only the Pro app plan as including commercial rights to generated worlds; nothing found for API-generated outputs. Read the API terms before any paid release README overstates 'fully meshed environment': code downloads only the collider mesh (a collision proxy) plus splats; the HQ mesh export is a separate $2.80 and the code does not call it Default object meshes are 50,000 faces with PBR: too heavy for phones and browser games; use LowPoly generate type and Blender cleanup. AI meshes are unrigged by default (Meshy option adds rigging) Price (fal and World Labs docs, Oct 2026, subject to change): world 1,500 credits = $1.20 (+80 credits pano = $0.064); Hunyuan3D v3 $0.375 base + $0.15 PBR + $0.15 custom face count = about $0.675 per object; Nano Banana 2 edit $0.08 (1K); SFX $0.002/s. A scene with 8 objects is roughly $7.50 first pass, before retries and Claude tokens Hunyuan via fal is listed as commercial use under fal terms; the open-weights Hunyuan licence excludes EU/UK/South Korea for self-hosting - fal's hosted route is the one priced here, but read fal terms before shipping Code quality: clean, modular, resumable (provider request id saved before polling), base64 stripped from logs, key in gitignored.env, typecheck passes (exit 0), 11 of 13 tests pass. BUT: zero timeouts or retries anywhere (two infinite polling loops), provider error bodies discarded (only the HTTP status is kept), ~4,100 lines of pipeline scripts with no tests, and the 2 failing tests only check that API keys are set Single maintainer, last commit 2026-05-14 (five months ago), 72 commits; 4.8k stars and 494 forks show interest, not production hardening Dependency licences checked: Spark, three, fiber, drei, leva, Radix, zustand MIT; postprocessing Zlib; the Rapier wrapper declares no licence field in its package.json (not checked further)

items.name: Papermorph
items.description: Claude Code skill (npx skills add DozenTwelve/Papermorph; 36 commits, 0 forks, no releases, one author) that turns a PDF into a static web book of chapters. Each chapter is a 1600x900 SVG 'stage' driven by a deterministic timeline: the narration is split into beats (mp3 + timed actions), [[mark]] tags in the script become word-start times from the TTS word boundaries, and every on-screen element (move, draw, pop, highlight, stream) is tweened from those times. Quiz cards (choice, blanks, grid, tap, sorter) sit between beats. No build step; progress saved in the browser. A review loop (contact-sheet screenshots, blank-opening checker, keyboard test, one fresh sub-agent per chapter with file-based state) is part of the skill. Visual style is a dark chalkboard.
items.verdictNote: ADD as a specialist tool for content studio plus a pattern source. Worth it for short, accurate, diagram-style explainers where a prompt-to-video model cannot be trusted with numbers or text (finance, math, rules of a game). Not a replacement for Seedance/Kling-style footage. Do not use as-is: it needs (1) the exporter step to become video, (2) a licensed or local voice instead of Edge TTS, (3) a small finance shape library. Pilot one finance-education explainer first, then decide.
items.why: RUN: the sample site loads and plays in this sandbox with no page errors; 42 frames viewed across a chapter. Narration quality and chapter-generation cost were NOT measured (no Opus tokens spent on generating a new chapter) IT IS A WEB BOOK, NOT A VIDEO TOOL. It has no export to MP4. I wrote a prototype exporter (tools/papermorph_render_beats.py): it opens a beat, calls the engine's own evalTo(t) for each frame, screenshots only the stage, and pipes frames plus the beat's mp3 into ffmpeg. Result: 1920x1080 30 fps MP4 with narration, deterministic and frame-exact. Speed here (CPU only): about 11 frames per second, roughly 2.6x real time, so a 5-minute lesson renders in about 13 minutes. Prototype: no resume, no caption burn-in, beats must be stitched with ffmpeg, tested on one beat of one chapter VOICE LICENCE RISK: narration uses Edge TTS, an unofficial route to Microsoft's Read Aloud service. A Microsoft Q&A moderator statement (Oct 2024) says commercial use without an Azure subscription may violate the terms. Swap before any monetised video: the local VoiceStudio/Supertonic tiers, Azure AI Speech, or ElevenLabs. The swap needs word timings for [[mark]] sync; VoiceStudio lists transcription but word-level timestamps are untested Young and tiny: 1 star, created recently, one maintainer; README says it currently supports Opus 5.5 only. Treat as a code-and-ideas source, pin a commit, expect breakage Quality is bounded by the model's storyboards: layouts are generated per chapter, so every chapter needs the review loop. Built for textbook math; finance visuals would need a helper library you do not have yet Opus-heavy by design (long skill, one sub-agent per chapter): token cost per minute of video is unknown. Measure on one pilot before planning volume MIT licence covers the code; any book/PDF you feed it keeps its own copyright, so only use your own scripts or public-domain/licensed text UPDATE Oct 13: HyperFrames (Apache-2.0, 59k stars) is a maintained renderer for HTML timelines and I ran it, so you should not maintain your own exporter for new explainers. Papermorph stays the pattern source for narration-mark timelines and interactive web lessons; its own engine (not GSAP) would need a small adapter to render through HyperFrames

items.name: Cloudflare security-audit skill
items.description: Single skill that turns a coding agent into a security auditor for one repo. Six phases: reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting by isolated agents, independent validation that tries to disprove every finding, schema-checked findings.json, re-verification, and a report. Covers web/auth, AI and prompt injection, supply chain, cloud, client-side and memory safety. Seed of Cloudflare's vulnerability harness. Last commit 2026-09-14.
items.verdictNote: adopt: run on your own repos before shipping anything public or paid
items.why: Defensive and well designed: a separate verifier must fail to disprove each finding, which cuts false alarms. Many sub-agents means a large token bill per run, so audit one repo at a time and re-run only on changes.

items.verdictNote: reference: only for authorized testing of systems you own or have written permission to test
items.why: Useful to understand how attackers approach your own stack, but it is attack methodology, not a defensive tool. For checking your own code, use the Cloudflare security-audit skill instead. Read install.sh before running it.

extra.note: Third-party price lists citing 4.x models were stale and dropped.

items.why: Not needed given Claude subscription; unverified reseller prices.

items.name: Qwen3.5 9B (Q4_K_M)
items.description: Top 8GB local pick (~5.7GB, ~38 tok/s); Qwen3.5 4B 2.7GB for CPU/long context.
items.why: Best local drafting model on the 4060; keep context 4-8K.

items.name: Gemma 4 (E4B / 12B QAT)
items.description: Writing-quality alternative; 12B QAT ~6.6GB, E4B small; sources conflict on sizes.
items.why: Try for prose; verify variant sizes.

items.name: Health Connect Jetpack client (androidx.health.connect:connect-client)
items.description: Android's on-device health data hub API: read/write steps, exercise, sleep, mindfulness sessions etc. 1.1.0 stable includes MindfulnessSessionRecord (WRITE_MINDFULNESS, experimental opt-in, needs FEATURE_MINDFULNESS_SESSION check).
items.why: Standard offline way for a native Android app to share fitness/mindful minutes with the rest of the phone; needs a privacy-rationale activity in the manifest.

items.name: Local Deep Research
items.description: Local multi-step research assistant with citations: quick summaries, detailed reports, document analysis over your own files (encrypted per-user SQLCipher library). Runs on Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp or vLLM, or cloud models; free search via SearXNG, arXiv, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, Wikipedia, GitHub; REST/Python API and a local STDIO MCP server for Claude Code. 8,270 commits, last commit 2026-10-16.
items.verdictNote: trial: research reports at $0 on a local 9B model
items.why: Fills the 'topic to cited report' step at zero API cost; self-reported SimpleQA 91.2% with Qwen3.5-9B (95.7% with a 27B model on a 24 GB card), small sample and LLM-graded. Docker on Windows needs the port-mapped compose; egress guard is best-effort and self-hosted SearXNG still forwards queries upstream; back up before upgrading (v1.10.7 warning).

items.name: React Three Rapier
items.description: Rapier (WASM) physics for React Three Fiber: rigid bodies, colliders, joints, collision events. v2 needs @react-three/fiber v9 and React 19 (v1 for React 18). Last commit 2025-11-03.
items.verdictNote: conditional on a React Three Fiber stack
items.why: Easiest physics for R3F games. Commit activity has slowed (last Nov 2025). For non-React three.js games use Rapier's own JS package directly.

items.name: Yuka
items.description: Engine-agnostic JavaScript game-AI library: state- and goal-driven agents, steering behaviours, graphs and navmesh pathfinding, perception with memory and vision, triggers, fuzzy logic, JSON save/load.
items.verdictNote: assess: good design, no commits since 2023
items.why: Works with any web engine, including a custom one. Last commit 2023-01-16, so expect no fixes; small and readable enough to vendor and maintain yourself if adopted.

items.name: three.quarks
items.description: Particle and VFX system for three.js (sparks, smoke, trails, magic) with a WYSIWYG editor at quarks.art that exports JSON. WebGPU rendering still on the roadmap. Last commit 2026-05-20.
items.why: Fills a real gap: designed effects without hand-writing shaders. Editor pricing not stated; WebGL only for now.

items.name: Colyseus
items.description: Authoritative multiplayer framework for Node.js: rooms, matchmaking, reconnection and automatic state sync, with client SDKs for JavaScript, Unity, Godot, Defold and Construct. Pre-1.0; last commit 2026-10-16.
items.verdictNote: assess when a multiplayer game is planned
items.why: MIT and self-hostable, so the cost is the server it runs on; the maintainers' paid Colyseus Cloud (pricing not shown) funds the project. Multiplayer adds hosting, cheating and moderation work: only worth it for a game designed around it.

items.name: Semantic Router
items.description: Routes a request to a predefined workflow by embedding similarity instead of asking an LLM to decide; works with local embedding models. Last commit 2026-10-19.
items.why: Replaces an LLM classification call with a near-free embedding lookup; needs good example utterances per route and a fallback when nothing matches.

items.name: RouteLLM
items.description: Trained routers that send easier prompts to a cheaper model and harder ones to a stronger model.
items.why: Last commit 2024-08-10; its routers were trained on an older strong/weak model pair. A rules-plus-fallback tier chain in LiteLLM is simpler and measurable.

items.name: GPTCache
items.description: Semantic cache for LLM answers: reuses a stored answer when a new request is similar enough. Last commit 2026-09-22.
items.verdictNote: assess: only for truly repetitive questions
items.why: A wrong 'similar enough' match returns a confidently stale or wrong answer. Use LiteLLM's built-in cache first; add semantic matching only where requests really repeat and freshness rules are clear.

items.name: requests-cache
items.description: Drop-in persistent cache for Python requests with expiry rules per URL. Last commit 2026-10-15.
items.why: One line stops scripts re-downloading the same public API data; set expiry per source so prices and news stay fresh.

items.name: Hishel
items.description: HTTP caching and revalidation (ETag/Last-Modified) for the Python httpx client. Last commit 2026-10-05.
items.why: Same job as requests-cache for httpx; pick the one matching the HTTP client a script already uses.

items.name: Chonkie
items.description: Lightweight document chunking library (token, sentence, semantic and other chunkers) for retrieval pipelines. Last commit 2026-08-26.
items.why: Sending the relevant chunks instead of whole documents is one of the largest token savings; only matters once there is a document-search step.

items.name: FlagEmbedding (BGE)
items.description: BAAI's BGE embedding and reranker models plus training code; rerankers re-score retrieved passages so only the strongest evidence reaches the prompt. Last commit 2026-08-24.
items.why: Reranking before generation cuts prompt size and improves accuracy. Check each model card's licence and VRAM; the smaller rerankers are expected to fit an 8 GB GPU (not measured).

items.name: LLMLingua
items.description: Microsoft's prompt compression (LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua, LLMLingua-2) that drops low-information tokens before the model reads them. Last commit 2026-09-10.
items.verdictNote: assess against a golden set first
items.why: Compression can silently drop numbers, negations and conditions. Only keep it where a before/after test on real tasks shows no accuracy loss; fix oversized inputs upstream first.

items.name: Prefect
items.description: Python workflow orchestration with retries, scheduling and task-result caching keyed on inputs; optional paid Prefect Cloud. Last commit 2026-10-19.
items.verdictNote: skip while n8n is the orchestrator
items.why: Good for code-heavy Python pipelines, but duplicates n8n plus a database job queue for a no-code-first setup.

items.name: Celery
items.description: Distributed Python task queue; needs a broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ. Last commit 2026-10-18.
items.why: Adds a broker to run and monitor; a database-backed job queue driven by n8n covers the same need at this scale.

items.name: APScheduler
items.description: In-process Python job scheduler (cron, interval, date triggers). Last commit 2026-10-13.
items.why: Handy inside a standalone Python script; n8n schedules already cover workflow timing.

items.name: PyBreaker
items.description: Circuit breaker for Python: stops calling a failing service after a threshold, then retries after a cool-off. Last commit 2026-09-25.
items.why: The pattern matters (stop runaway retry loops); for model calls LiteLLM's allowed-fails and cooldown settings already do it. Use PyBreaker only for non-LLM services called from Python.

items.name: Portkey Gateway
items.description: Open-source AI gateway with routing, fallbacks, retries and caching across many providers; hosted Portkey adds paid features. Last commit 2026-05-25.
items.why: Overlaps LiteLLM almost entirely; running two gateways doubles the configuration for no saving.

items.name: Listmonk
items.why: Self-hosted newsletter and mailing-list manager already running for several brands; pair it with an external SMTP provider (SES/SMTP2GO) plus SPF/DKIM/DMARC.

items.name: short-video-maker
items.why: Open-source short-video assembler (Kokoro TTS, Whisper captions, Remotion) that matches our local stack; check how actively it is maintained and Remotion's licence terms.

items.name: PocketBase
items.why: Single Go binary (SQLite) providing auth, storage, realtime and a REST API in about 30 MB; a lighter backend option for new small apps than a full Supabase stack.

items.name: Ruflo (formerly Claude Flow)
items.description: Agent 'meta-harness' for Claude Code and Codex, renamed from claude-flow: 100+ agents, swarm topologies, vector memory, federation across machines, a large MCP server (about 300 tools) and hundreds of skills. Installs via npx or a Claude Code plugin. Very active (commit 2026-10-24).
items.verdictNote: reference: study the swarm and memory patterns; don't install into your main setup
items.why: Huge surface and many claims (routing accuracy, security hardening) with no evidence on the page; the README itself says plugins run unsandboxed with your permissions. Hundreds of MCP tools also bloat every session's context. Claude Code's own sub-agents cover most needs for less.

items.name: CLI-Anything
items.description: Generates agent-friendly command-line interfaces for existing desktop software, with structured output. CLI-Hub installs community harnesses for Blender, ComfyUI, Audacity, QGIS, Calibre, Dify, ChromaDB and more; a seven-phase pipeline builds new ones from source. Plugins for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex. Last commit 2026-09-22.
items.verdictNote: trial: try one ready-made harness (Blender or ComfyUI) before generating your own
items.why: Lets an agent drive creative apps without screen clicking, which is cheaper and more reliable than computer use. Harness quality varies by contributor (research-lab project), so test each one on a throwaway file first.

items.name: ai-memory
items.description: Shared long-term memory for coding agents: a git-backed wiki of plain markdown (source of truth) plus a rebuildable SQLite search index. Works with 20+ harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Kiro) via MCP or hooks. Rust single binary or Docker; Linux and macOS, Windows through WSL2. Optional LLM or embedding API keys. Last commit 2026-10-22.
items.verdictNote: assess: worth it only if you switch between several coding agents and want one memory
items.why: Sound design: readable markdown in git, so nothing is locked in a database. Adds a service to run, and native Windows is experimental. If you mostly use one agent, its built-in memory or a CLAUDE.md is simpler.

items.name: Context Mode
items.description: MCP server plus hooks that keep large tool outputs (logs, web pages, Playwright snapshots, issue lists) out of the agent's context: commands run in a sandboxed subprocess, results are indexed in local SQLite full-text search, and only matching snippets come back. Also logs session events so the agent can recover after compaction. Supports Claude Code and 16 other agents; best with Claude Code hooks. Vendor claims up to 98% context savings (not independently verified). Very active (commit 2026-10-24).
items.verdictNote: trial: one week on a long Claude Code project; compare session length and cost
items.why: Targets the real cost driver in long agent sessions: bulky tool output. Everything stays local. Elastic License 2.0 is fine for your own use but forbids offering it to others as a hosted service.

items.name: agentic-framework (JeweledTech)
items.description: Python framework that arranges AI agents into business departments (sales, marketing, engineering, support, back office) with optional CrewAI, a FastAPI server, Docker, a demo UI and a library of n8n workflow templates. About 24 commits; last commit 2026-05-12.
items.verdictNote: skip: early, stale since May and marketing-heavy
items.why: Headline numbers (departments, 87 workflows) are unproven and there's an enterprise upsell. Claude's plugins plus n8n give the same department setup with less code to maintain. The n8n templates may be worth a look.

items.name: AI-Powered-Digital-Marketing-Agency (Amanux7)
items.description: Small prototype: React/Vite front end and one Python file where specialist agents draft marketing work that an 'AI CMO' agent reviews. 11 files, 4 commits; last 2026-01-09.
items.why: Only the reviewer-agent idea is worth keeping (one agent checks the others before delivery); there's nothing here to install.

items.name: ruvnet/marketing (AI marketing swarm)
items.description: TypeScript system of 15 agents in five tiers (coordination, intelligence, creative, attribution, operations) meant to run ad campaigns across Google Ads, Meta, TikTok and others, built on the Claude Flow (Ruflo) framework. About 18k lines of source; 18 commits; last commit 2026-05-23. Needs an Anthropic API key and ad-platform credentials.
items.verdictNote: reference: borrow the agent tiers and the quality-gate idea; never connect a live ad account
items.why: It is designed to change bids, budgets and creatives on real ad accounts, and the README doesn't show how human approval works. Superlatives and performance figures come with no evidence, and nothing has changed since May. Depends on the external Claude Flow package.

items.name: Marketing Dashboard (Builderz Labs)
items.description: Self-hosted marketing operations dashboard: CRM leads and pipeline, outreach sequences, content calendar with approval queues, KPI views, cron automations and AI-agent activity in one screen. Next.js 16 plus local SQLite, no hosted backend; optional connectors for Plausible, GA4, X, LinkedIn, Gmail and Mailchimp, and OpenClaw agents. Alpha status; 47 commits; last 2026-09-22.
items.verdictNote: assess: good fit if you want one approval screen for agent-made content; wait for a beta
items.why: Free, local-first, and built around human approval before anything posts, which is the right control for automated content. But it's alpha (schemas may change), needs Node and pnpm to run, and you'd have to change the seeded login before exposing it anywhere.

items.name: Kronos (financial candle foundation model)
items.description: Open foundation model that tokenizes OHLCV market candles and generates probabilistic future price paths. Open weights: Kronos-mini (4.1M params, 2048 context), small (24.7M) and base (102.3M), both 512 context; large (499M) is closed. Includes fine-tuning on Qlib data and a demo backtest. Paper accepted at AAAI 2026.
items.verdictNote: assess: good for education visuals and research; no proven trading edge
items.why: Small enough to run on an 8 GB laptop GPU, and its fan of sampled price paths makes a great 'range of outcomes' visual. The README itself says it is not a production trading system: signals still need risk controls, costs and slippage, and the README shows no live performance.

items.name: TradingAgents (TauricResearch)
items.description: Multi-agent LLM framework that mimics a trading firm: fundamentals, news, sentiment and technical analysts, bull and bear researchers who debate, a trader, a risk team and a portfolio manager. Works with most LLM providers or local Ollama; data from Alpha Vantage (key), FRED, SEC EDGAR. v0.7.0 (2026-10) adds a resumable backtest grid scored on alpha against a benchmark.
items.verdictNote: assess: copy the debate-and-risk-review pattern; don't trade its signals
items.why: The analyst, debate and risk-manager structure is a strong pattern for any research workflow. But it is research-only by its own disclaimer, each run costs many LLM calls, and backtests on past dates are contaminated because the LLM already 'knows' what happened after its training data.

items.name: print3d (mfranzon)
items.description: Agent plugin (Hermes Agent, also Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI) that turns an idea, a photo or a shop listing into a sliced Bambu Studio .3mf: the agent writes a Blender script, the plugin checks the mesh, slices it, and loops until checks pass. Needs Blender 4.2+, Bambu Studio and uv. Only one printer profile: Bambu Lab X2D, 0.4 mm nozzle. Last commit 2026-10-23.
items.verdictNote: reference: copy the build-check-fix loop; use text-to-cad for real parts
items.why: The loop (generate, check, slice, fix) is a smart design. But it is brand new (5 stars), supports only one Bambu printer, and makes meshes rather than editable CAD; text-to-cad is more mature and also hands off to Bambu printers.

items.name: Fieldwatch
items.description: Android 10+ app (sideloaded APK, not on Play) that passively lists nearby Wi-Fi access points and Bluetooth LE devices, with filters, a device-signature library, 'co-travel' alerts and offline reports. No account, no server; formerly called Spectre. Last commit 2026-10-23.
items.verdictNote: reference: useful to check what's broadcasting around you (e.g. unknown trackers)
items.why: Receive-only and offline, which is the safe design. Matches are guesses, not identification. Logs keep exact locations, so guard the files, and don't use it to track people; that can be illegal. Sideloading means you trust the author's APK.

items.verdictNote: adopt: main discovery list for Claude Code skills, hooks and tools
items.why: About 280 curated entries, updated 2026-10-24. Submissions go through a form checked by a bot, not a quality review, so vet each tool. Licence is NonCommercial-NoDerivatives: link to it, don't copy its contents into another published list.

items.why: Handy browsing; not affiliated with Anthropic.

items.why: Canonical discovery source for MCP servers.

items.name: punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers
items.description: Large categorized list of MCP servers, linked to glama.ai/mcp/servers.
items.why: Largest MCP index; use to find YouTube/video/image/social servers.

items.name: Glama MCP multimedia category
items.description: Glama directory category for multimedia MCP servers.
items.why: Browse for vetted media servers.

items.name: Glama MCP servers directory
items.description: MCP server directory backing awesome-mcp-servers.
items.why: Search for YouTube/social MCPs.

items.name: awesome-motion-design-agent-skills
items.description: A map of 5 first-party skills, 10 engine projects (GSAP, Motion, R3F, Remotion, Anime.js, Rive, dotLottie, Phaser) and 7 third-party packs, with link checks and advice to scan third-party packs before installing. Search also showed a larger catalogue, zhuyansen/awesome-claude-video-skills (about 180 repos, each security-graded): not opened.
items.verdictNote: REFERENCE: use as a directory; never install from a list without reading the skill.
items.why: 2 stars; counts are 'discovery signals, not rankings'
items.source: research 2026-10: content, motion, 3D and game tools

items.name: awesome-selfhosted
items.description: The main directory of free software you can run on your own server (about 1,400 linked projects): automation, analytics, media, CRM, docs, mail, monitoring and more, each with licence and language. Last commit 2026-10-22.
items.verdictNote: adopt: first stop before paying for a SaaS tool
items.why: Best source of self-hostable alternatives (n8n, Postiz-style schedulers, analytics) to keep monthly costs down. Being listed is not a review: check each project's activity, licence and security before running it on a server.

items.name: awesome-python
items.description: Curated list of Python frameworks, libraries and tools by category (about 560 links): web, data, scraping, CLI, testing, ML and more. Last commit 2026-10-23.
items.verdictNote: adopt: reference when Claude writes Python
items.why: Useful for picking a well-known library instead of an obscure one when automation scripts are built in Python. A directory, not a quality ranking.

items.name: The Book of Secret Knowledge
items.description: Large collection of command-line tools, one-liners, cheat sheets, blogs and security resources for sysadmins and DevOps.
items.why: Handy for server and network troubleshooting, but last commit 2024-11-19, so some links and tools are stale. Includes offensive-security tools: use those only on systems you own or are authorised to test.

items.name: awesome-go
items.description: Curated list of Go frameworks, libraries and software (about 3,000 links), with quality requirements for new entries. Last commit 2026-10-23.
items.verdictNote: reference: only if a project is written in Go
items.why: Well maintained, but current projects use Node.js and Python; useful mainly when choosing Go-based self-hosted tools.

items.name: awesome-nodejs
items.description: Curated Node.js packages and resources by category (CLI, HTTP, databases, testing, scraping and more) from Sindre Sorhus. Last commit 2026-09-02.
items.verdictNote: adopt: reference when Claude writes Node.js
items.why: Node.js runs the MCP servers and most scripts, and this list is strictly curated, so it's a good place to pick dependable packages.

items.name: awesome-cpp
items.description: Large curated list of C/C++ frameworks, libraries and resources (about 1,400 links), including embedded, audio, graphics, networking and game sections. Last commit 2026-10-10.
items.verdictNote: reference: for firmware and embedded projects
items.why: Useful when microcontroller or device firmware (ESP32/Arduino) needs a C++ library; not needed for web or Python work.

items.name: awesome-react
items.description: Curated React ecosystem list: tutorials, state management, routing, UI, testing, frameworks. Last commit 2026-09-04.
items.why: Good map of the React ecosystem when a website or React Three Fiber game is built; the licence is inconsistent, so link to it rather than copy.
items.license: unclear (badge says CC0, links CC BY 4.0; no LICENSE file)

items.name: awesome-react-components

assessments.title: Deep assessments
assessments.description: Repos and models evaluated in depth, with warnings and what to steal.

items.name: atlas-gic
items.description: Self-improving trading agent framework: 4 agent layers, evolutionary prompt selection scored by Sharpe ratio, regime-specific cohorts, automatic specialist spawning. Claude Sonnet + FMP/Finnhub/Polygon/FRED.
items.verdictNote: steal the architecture, do not deploy
why: Prompt variants competing on a measured score (same idea as dspy + golden set)
Automatic retirement of bottom performers, which our Improver only suggests today
Spawn a specialist when the same gap repeats - a clean trigger rule for the swarm
Regime-specific cohorts: a prompt tuned in one regime is not tuned for another

warnings: The +22% over 173 days backtest is self-reported, unaudited, single-window; stars do not validate returns
Autonomous self-improving loop next to real money is the highest risk category in this brief
Apply the selection loop to extraction accuracy, listings and content - not to a live account

items.name: threejs-particle-fluids
items.description: MIT-licensed GPU particle fluid/cloth/smoke simulation in Three.js using WebGPU and TSL; nine presets, live controls, perf diagnostics; CC0 bundled assets
why: Effects technique and preset structure for future visual work

warnings: WebGPU mandatory with NO WebGL fallback - disqualifying for indie browser games that must run on phones and older laptops
4 stars, 0 forks: unproven
Revisit when WebGPU support is broad enough that no fallback is needed

items.name: Jev ecosystem (agents/memory/safety/tools/open models)
items.description: Official TypeSafe org publishes JS and Python SDKs, an agent-skills repo and system-one-adapter-python, each at roughly 15-35 stars. Community projects listed by the user arrived truncated and could not be opened.
why: typesafe-ai/system-one-adapter-python: drop-in TypeSafe client backed by ordinary LLM APIs - design and test the Jev gate against the golden set using Haiku BEFORE buying a key or adding a sixth vendor

warnings: Jev launched 2026-09-15; every project here is at most two weeks old
Memory/compaction projects overlap decisions already made (Supabase canonical, one memory layer)
Guard project overlaps our accuracy guard
Open-model clones matter only if Jev pricing or access changes
jev-trader carries the same live-money warning as atlas-gic
Community links unverified - treat awesome-lists as a map of attempts, not recommendations

items.name: UniMate (articulated motion generation)
items.url: https://linzhanmou.com/unimate/ ; arXiv 2609.05415 ; code MIT, weights+dataset on HuggingFace
items.description: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 paper (Princeton/UC Berkeley/MIT). Rigged 3D asset + text prompt -> motion for ARBITRARY skeletons, no per-skeleton fine-tuning. Topology-aware diffusion transformer trained on UniML3D (13,006 sequences, creatures and objects). Zero-shot motion editing, in-betweening, expansion.
items.verdictNote: high potential for indie 3D games, blocked on training-data licensing
why: Targets indie-game's most expensive step: animation, which is the hard part of a weekly release cadence
Arbitrary skeletons is the key differentiator - most motion models are human-mocap only and cannot animate a dragon, cat or mech
Zero-shot in-betweening and editing would cut per-asset animation work substantially if clearable

warnings: MIT code does NOT make the weights commercially clear: training data is Mixamo (Adobe terms) + Objaverse-XL (per-object licences) + Truebones ZOO (commercial licence); repo instructs users to comply with source licences
Selling a game containing this model's output is an unsettled question - needs a lawyer before any paid release; answer may differ for free portal vs paid Steam
BLOCKING UNKNOWN: is the target game 2D or 3D? If 2D sprite games, skeletal motion synthesis is irrelevant
VRAM requirements unstated; diffusion transformer on an 8GB 4060 shared with ComfyUI and VoiceStudio is not a safe assumption
Export format unverified - value depends on glTF/FBX/BVH importing cleanly into a custom web engine or Godot
Posted ~2026-09-14, roughly two weeks old; research code, not a production dependency for weekly shipping
extra.unblockedAlternative: Mixamo's own library is free and explicitly licensed for commercial game use (humanoid). For non-humanoid, hand-authored Blender cycles or procedural animation; a small reusable cycle library beats an unclearable research model for a weekly cadence.

items.name: AERIS-10 (PLFM_RADAR)
items.description: Open-source 10.5 GHz PLFM phased array radar; 3 km and 20 km variants; +/-45 deg electronic beam steering, 360 deg mechanical scan; Xilinx XC7A50T FPGA + STM32F746; Python GUI with maps; GPS/IMU. Alpha / work in progress.
why: Requires custom multi-layer RF PCBs at 10.5 GHz vs current off-the-shelf ESP32/nRF52840 modules
Requires VHDL/Verilog FPGA work; user prefers no-code and has negligible coding experience
Requires VNA and spectrum analyser past 10 GHz; thousands in parts plus test gear
25.4k stars against 348 commits and Alpha badge: viral ahead of maturity, designs unproven

legalBlockers: Transmitting at 10.5 GHz with PAs at km range is not licence-exempt in Canada; verify with ISED licence-exempt standards; amateur licence is the only realistic hobby route
Radar is dual-use; a 20 km phased array may fall under Canada's Export Control List, restricting kit sales, board shipping and cross-border design-file sharing
patternsToSteal: CERN-OHL-P (hardware) + MIT (software) licence split - copy for the LoRa find-my-car release
Two-tier product ladder (short-range / long-range from one architecture) as the kit pricing model
Python GUI with map integration - reusable for the find-my-car tracker UI
GPS + IMU fusion pattern - same problem the tracker solves
Open-hardware repo structure: docs layout, contribution guidelines, status badges

items.name: RSIGame
items.description: Paper arXiv 2609.39045 (Sept 30 2026) + Apache-2.0 repo (28k lines Python). Loop per round: Explore (agent plays the built game, records logs/frames) -> Diagnose (one objective with most headroom) -> Edit (repair agent) -> Verify (independent agent replays; did it land, did anything regress). Outer 'Global Quality Monitor' keeps the best checkpoint and stops after K=3 checkpoints with no new champion. Evolving checklist of what the task asked for. Targets Godot 4 and Phaser. Second half: distils successful sessions into a LoRA on Qwen3.8-27B.
items.verdictNote: reference, not adopt-to-run. Steal five patterns now; revisit the code if weights/corpus are released and indie web-game games run on Godot.
items.why: Champion + saturation stop: keep the best build seen; stop after 3 checkpoints with no improvement. Apply to every swarm self-improve loop (Printables, finance-education shorts, indie web-game polish) - caps token spend and prevents late rounds undoing earlier gains Independent verifier: the agent that checks a change is not the one that made it, and must test for regressions, not just 'did it work' 'Silence does not write' checklist: an item not observed this round keeps its status; only evidence moves it. Fixes oscillating scores from noisy LLM judges (they measured 10% of items flipping between readings of the same trace) One objective per round: diagnose the single place with most headroom, edit against that only Cost metering through one loopback proxy that logs every call (prompt/completion/cached/reasoning tokens, dollars). A LiteLLM router with a cost-logging table already does the same; confirm cached and reasoning tokens are captured Hygiene to copy into Claude Code handoff: 'rsigame check' preflight before a run; test that scans the repo for secrets/personal paths; test that resolves every import including those inside functions; 3-layer config (defaults -> experiment -> env)

warnings: Numbers are the authors' own, on their own benchmark (GameCraft-Bench, 140 tasks), scored by an LLM judge; no independent reproduction yet. Repo has 6 stars and is 2 days old

Headline 'Qwen3.8-27B beats GPT-5.5 one-shot, 11x fewer generation tokens' needs 4x H100 80GB training and is about generation tokens after fine-tuning, not total loop cost. Not reproducible on an an 8 GB GPU
Weights, supervised corpus and base games are 'coming soon' pending the authors' company review; only table artefacts are published

`rsigame develop <game>` only accepts names from the benchmark's tasks/ folder (141 tasks). Running it on an existing game means writing them up as benchmark tasks (spec, base project, scripted demo inputs) - unverified how much work

Needs Godot 4 (or Node + OpenGame for Phaser) and an OpenRouter key; indie web-game in-house a custom web game engine is not supported without writing an adapter (the authors say the engine-specific part is ~900 of 48k lines)
No cost-per-game figure published. Their runs were 30-64 rounds with up to 1800 s repair budgets; run one game with a hard spend cap before committing

Code quality: strong design documentation and tests of the key logic, but declared Python >=3.11 while project_map.py uses 3.12-only f-string syntax (fails to compile on 3.11 and breaks 2 tests); ~6 undefined-name bugs in rarely-run scripts; huge functions (one_round 398 lines, explore 408); only ~1k lines of tests for 28k of source
Dependency licences checked: GameCraft-Bench Apache-2.0, OpenGame Apache-2.0 (per authors' NOTICE, not independently opened)

items.name: Only your own software, hardware and builds, or a client's with written authorisation
items.description: Only your own software, hardware and builds, or a client's with written authorisation. Canada's Copyright Act s.41.12 allows getting around a technological protection measure on a LAWFULLY OBTAINED program only to achieve interoperability, and the exemption is lost if it is used to infringe. App/game terms of service often forbid reverse engineering even where the law allows it.
items.why: Run RE tools only in an isolated VM, never on a production server or a machine holding API keys; never add a reverse-engineered private API to the public API catalogue; keep a one-line written purpose for each RE job; not legal advice: ask a lawyer before any client RE engagement.

items.name: agentSkill note 1

items.name: agentSkill note 3
items.description: Install safety: read SKILL.md fully, install per-project, pin a commit, never load unvetted skills in a session holding Supabase service keys or API keys, review diffs before updating.

items.name: agentSkill note 4

items.name: agentSkill note 5

items.description: Verified 2026-09-17: obra/superpowers ships via Anthropic's official plugin marketplace; steveyegge/beads is a git-backed issue tracker for agents. The other 38 were not individually verified.

items.name: agentToolkit note 2
items.description: Adopt order: superpowers, beads, serena, repomix, planning-with-files, karpathy-skills, codex-plugin-cc, taste-skill, addyosmani skills, mattpocock skills, claude-hud, rtk.

items.description: Risk: headroom/rtk/caveman compress context or output; the accuracy guard rejects numbers missing from source, so never use them on the daily data pipeline or publishing paths.

items.name: agentToolkit note 4

items.name: agentToolkit note 5

items.name: agentToolkit note 6

items.name: agentFramework note 1
items.description: Filter: orchestration stays in n8n, routing in LiteLLM, state in Supabase, building in Claude Code. A framework must do something that stack cannot.

items.name: agentFramework note 2

items.name: agentFramework note 3

items.name: agentFramework note 4

items.name: agentFramework note 5

items.name: agentFramework note 6

items.name: designResource note 1
items.description: Platform mismatch is the whole issue with Webflow/Framer template libraries: they do not produce code that lands in artifacts or Vercel.

items.name: designResource note 2
items.description: Price is not a design property. What reads as expensive: restraint, typography, generous spacing, ONE memorable motion moment, real content instead of placeholder copy.

items.name: designResource note 3
items.description: A template tends to produce a site that looks like that template - which works against premium positioning for a finance-education brand, where the pitch is being different.

items.name: designResource note 4
items.description: The artifact-design skill (already in stack) and taste-skill (on the adopt list) target design judgement more directly than any component purchase.

items.name: designResource note 5
items.description: For client work where the client wants to self-edit afterwards, a Webflow template library becomes genuinely useful - a real scenario for consulting clients only.

items.name: design-resource note batch2-3 #1
items.description: Batch 2 (Oct 9, 2026): 25 sites checked. Already on the list and unchanged: Aceternity UI and Magic UI (adopt). Of the 23 new entries, 12 are adopt, 9 are reference, hold or experimental, and 2 are skip.

items.name: design-resource note batch2-3 #2
items.description: Artifact test: the pages are single self-contained HTML files. Only copy-paste CSS/SVG (Uiverse, CSS Text Effects, MicroKit CSS, Circle Loaders) and one-script-tag libraries (Anime.js) drop straight in. React/Tailwind catalogues (shadcn, 21st.dev, Motion Primitives, mapcn) need a Vercel project with a build step.

items.name: design-resource note batch2-3 #3
items.description: Inspiration galleries (Minimal Gallery, Kage, Refero, AppShot, Component Gallery) show other people's copyrighted designs. Use them to choose a direction and write your own DESIGN.md; never reproduce a real brand or site.

items.name: design-resource note batch2-3 #4
items.description: Licence reality: MIT is stated by Uiverse, CSS Text Effects, MicroKit, shadcn, Anime.js, Motion Primitives, mapcn and Liquid Glass. CC0 is stated by Kitbitz and 3dicons. Kinetics, Circle Loaders, Gradient Buttons, Jiro, Kage, VibePrompt, Refero and Component Gallery state no usable licence: treat as reference until confirmed.

items.name: design-resource note batch2-3 #5
items.description: The biggest find is not a gallery: it is Google's DESIGN.md format (Apache-2.0, alpha). One DESIGN.md per venture, linted for contrast, is the cheapest route to consistent output across pages, Shorts frames and PDFs.

items.name: design-resource note batch2-3 #6
items.description: Prompt libraries (Jiro, VibePrompt, Kage prompts) sell something Claude already does well. The scarce asset is a consistent brand spec, not another prompt.

items.name: design-resource note batch2-3 #7
items.description: Map caveat: mapcn defaults to CARTO basemaps, whose commercial use needs an Enterprise licence per the README; pick another MapLibre-compatible tile source before monetising.

items.name: design-resource note batch2-3 #8
items.description: Batch 3 (Oct 13, 2026), for the upcoming websites: 8 sites checked; 3 were already listed (Minimal Gallery, Refero Styles, 3dicons). Of 5 new: Awwwards, Godly/Recent and Supahero added as free references; Scrolltide on hold ($299, same libraries as the free kit); Mobbin skipped for websites (app-UI library, paid). Workflow for a new site: browse Awwwards (filter GSAP/Three.js) + Supahero + Minimal Gallery, pick ONE direction, write the site's DESIGN.md, build with the free kit.

items.name: gpu vram note #1
items.description: Rule on 8 GB: ONE heavy GPU job at a time. Qwen, Flux, VoiceStudio, Whisper and Stable Fast 3D each want most of the card; the job worker should unload Ollama (keep_alive 0) and restart voice between batches.

items.name: gpu vram note #2
items.description: Use now on 8 GB: Qwen 3.5 9B, VoiceStudio (with restarts), Kokoro, Whisper turbo/small, Flux Q4 GGUF, Stable Fast 3D, Blender + blender-mcp, HyperFrames. Cloud for the rest: TRELLIS.2 on fal, Seedance/Hailuo video.

items.name: gpu vram note #3
items.description: Unlocks at 24 GB, in priority order: (1) Flux FP8 with LoRAs/ControlNet for brand-consistent images, (2) TRELLIS.2 locally (needs Linux), (3) Qwen-Image + AnyAngle multi-angle shots, (4) H3 motion chaining, (5) Whisper large alongside other jobs, (6) bigger local LLM / QLoRA.

items.name: gpu vram note #4
items.description: A 24 GB card does NOT fix licence blockers: Hunyuan3D and HY-World stay excluded for worldwide display; UniMate stays blocked on training-data licences.

items.name: gpu vram note #5
items.description: Open question for the upgrade: where will the 24 GB card live (desktop PC, eGPU, or cloud) and on Windows or Linux? TRELLIS.2 officially supports Linux only.

items.name: gpu vram note #6
items.description: Oct 13 game-studio batch: ACE-Step 1.5 is usable now on 8 GB (music). Catalogued for later: Audio2Face (3D characters), Matrix-Game 5B (concept footage). Beyond reach even at 24 GB: Hunyuan-GameCraft (80 GB recommended).

items.name: VRAM: Qwen 3.5 9B (Ollama)
items.description: Qwen 3.5 9B (Ollama) (Local LLM): needs Fits an 8 GB GPU today at 100% GPU (your own requirement). Exact GB at the quantisation not measured. On 8 GB: Keep as the local ops model; unload it (keep_alive 0) before ComfyUI or voice jobs. At 24 GB: Room for a bigger local model or longer context; pick after measuring quality on the golden set.

extra.source: brain: infrastructure.machines (local machine constraint 'must show 100% GPU')

items.name: VRAM: VoiceStudio / OmniVoice
items.description: VoiceStudio / OmniVoice (Voice): needs About 1 GB at load (third-party estimate, Spheron). Open bug: memory grows with each call (one user saw 5 GB to nearly 20 GB over 3 weeks). On 8 GB: Use it, but restart the voice model between batches or apply the empty_cache +.cpu workaround; never leave it running beside Flux. At 24 GB: Headroom hides the leak but does not fix it: keep the restart rule.

items.name: VRAM: Kokoro TTS
items.description: Kokoro TTS (Voice): needs Small; also runs on CPU (not measured). On 8 GB: Drafts and fallback. At 24 GB: No change.

items.name: VRAM: Supertonic 3
items.description: Supertonic 3 (Voice): needs CPU only (runs on a production server). On 8 GB: Fallback voice on a production server. At 24 GB: No change.

items.name: VRAM: Whisper (speech to text, word timestamps)
items.description: Whisper (speech to text, word timestamps) (Transcription): needs tiny/base ~1 GB, small ~2 GB, medium ~5 GB, turbo ~6 GB, large ~10 GB. On 8 GB: turbo (~6 GB) or small (~2 GB) for caption and voice-over timing; run alone on the card. At 24 GB: large (~10 GB) alongside other jobs.

items.name: VRAM: FLUX.1 dev (ComfyUI images)
items.description: FLUX.1 dev (ComfyUI images) (Images): needs FP16 24 GB, FP8 ~13 GB, GGUF Q4_0 ~7 GB. On 8 GB: GGUF Q4_0 only; slow (about 1m42s per 1024px image listed for a 4060); one LoRA at a time. At 24 GB: FP8 (~13 GB) with LoRAs and a ControlNet (~3.6 GB each); FP16 only just fits.

items.name: VRAM: Stable Fast 3D
items.description: Stable Fast 3D (3D assets): needs ~6 GB. On 8 GB: Free local image-to-3D for quick props and greybox. At 24 GB: Keep as the fast draft step before TRELLIS.2. Beyond VRAM: Stability Community Licence: register, show 'Powered by Stability AI', free under $1M revenue

items.name: VRAM: HyperFrames / HTML-to-video exporters (video rendering)
items.description: HyperFrames / HTML-to-video exporters (video rendering) (Video render): needs No GPU needed (headless Chrome + ffmpeg; ~256 MB RAM per worker). On 8 GB: Use now. At 24 GB: GPU encoding/faster capture possible; not needed.

items.name: VRAM: blender-mcp + Blender
items.description: blender-mcp + Blender (3D clean-up): needs Blender viewport works on 8 GB; heavy Cycles renders slower. On 8 GB: Use now for mesh clean-up and GLB export. At 24 GB: Faster Cycles renders.

items.name: VRAM: TRELLIS.2 (Microsoft)
items.description: TRELLIS.2 (Microsoft) (3D assets): needs At least 24 GB (official); tested on A100/H100. On 8 GB: Use hosted on fal ($0.25-0.35 per model). At 24 GB: Run locally IF the machine runs Linux (official support is Linux only; Windows/WSL untested). Beyond VRAM: Linux only

items.name: VRAM: Qwen-Image-2.1 + AnyAngle LoRA
items.description: Qwen-Image-2.1 + AnyAngle LoRA (Images (multi-angle)): needs ~16 GB. On 8 GB: Skip (GGUF quants exist but quality drops and minutes per image). At 24 GB: Unlock: multi-angle product and character shots locally.

items.name: VRAM: H3 motion-context chaining (ComfyUI)
items.description: H3 motion-context chaining (ComfyUI) (Video): needs Documented floor: a heavily offloaded 12 GB card. On 8 GB: Keep the small-chunk workflow (owner decision). At 24 GB: Revisit: local H3 with motion-context chaining. Beyond VRAM: Open-weight H3 licence excludes US/EU/UK/South Korea; read before publishing

items.name: VRAM: Hunyuan3D-2.1 (open weights)
items.description: Hunyuan3D-2.1 (open weights) (3D assets): needs 10 GB shape, 21 GB texture, 29 GB both. On 8 GB: Skip; use TRELLIS.2 on fal. At 24 GB: Technically fits shape+texture in two passes. Beyond VRAM: Licence excludes EU/UK/South Korea, including displaying outputs there: still skip after the upgrade

items.name: VRAM: HY-World 2.0 (Tencent)
items.description: HY-World 2.0 (Tencent) (3D worlds): needs Not published; paper: ~10 minutes per scene on a data-centre H20. On 8 GB: Skip. At 24 GB: Probably still too heavy; re-check if a consumer version ships. Beyond VRAM: Same territory licence as Hunyuan

items.name: VRAM: UniMate (motion for any skeleton)
items.description: UniMate (motion for any skeleton) (3D animation): needs Not stated (diffusion transformer). On 8 GB: Skip. At 24 GB: Re-check VRAM once licensing is cleared. Beyond VRAM: Training-data licences (Mixamo etc.) block commercial use

items.name: VRAM: Local fine-tuning (QLoRA)
items.description: Local fine-tuning (QLoRA) (Training): needs 4B QLoRA fits on 8 GB. On 8 GB: 4B QLoRA only. At 24 GB: Larger-model QLoRA (size to be measured, not assumed).

items.name: VRAM: RSIGame-style self-improving training
items.description: RSIGame-style self-improving training (Training): needs 4x H100 80 GB in the paper. On 8 GB: Skip. At 24 GB: Still out of reach at 24 GB; cloud only.

items.name: VRAM: ACE-Step 1.5 (music)
items.description: ACE-Step 1.5 (music) (Music): needs Under 4 GB minimum (offload); 6-8 GB tier = 2B turbo + 0.6B LM; XL needs 20-24 GB without offload. On 8 GB: Use the 2B turbo tier for soundtracks and Shorts beds. At 24 GB: XL models for higher quality.

items.name: VRAM: HunyuanVideo-Foley (video to SFX)
items.description: HunyuanVideo-Foley (video to SFX) (Sound effects): needs XL 16 GB (8 GB with offload); XXL 20 GB (12 GB with offload). On 8 GB: Technically fits with offload, but skip. At 24 GB: Fits without offload. Beyond VRAM: Tencent licence excludes EU/UK/South Korea: skip regardless of VRAM

items.name: VRAM: Audio2Face-3D (lip-sync)
items.description: Audio2Face-3D (lip-sync) (3D animation): needs Not stated (CPU fallback exists). On 8 GB: Not needed yet (no 3D talking characters). At 24 GB: Re-check when 3D characters arrive.

items.name: VRAM: Hunyuan-GameCraft 1.0
items.description: Hunyuan-GameCraft 1.0 (Game video): needs 24 GB minimum 'very slow'; 80 GB recommended. On 8 GB: Skip. At 24 GB: Still impractical; cloud or skip. Beyond VRAM: Tencent licence

items.name: VRAM: Matrix-Game 3.0
items.description: Matrix-Game 3.0 (World video): needs Not published (5B model, 720p; multi-GPU examples). On 8 GB: Skip. At 24 GB: Test the 5B model for trailer/concept footage.

items.name: Instagram Trial Reels via publishing API
items.description: Official Instagram Graph API supports trial Reels (shown to non-followers first) via trial_params on the media container; 100 API posts per 24h per account.

items.name: Instagram API with Instagram Login
items.description: Business-type Meta app + instagram_business_basic/instagram_business_content_publish; container -> poll FINISHED -> media_publish; media must be a public URL (resumable local upload is Facebook-Login only).
items.why: Simplest official IG auto-posting path: no Facebook Page needed, graph.instagram.com, dashboard 'Generate token' gives a 60-day token refreshable via refresh_access_token; App Review only for Advanced Access (other people's accounts).

items.name: Upload-Post
items.why: Cheap unified posting API to bridge the gap while our own YouTube/TikTok/Meta API audits are pending; the platform count it claims is inconsistent, so verify per platform.

items.name: Late (getlate.dev)
items.why: Flat-priced single API for ~13 social platforms; an alternative posting bridge, pricing not yet confirmed.

items.name: Blotato
items.why: Posts to TikTok through an already-audited app, which may avoid the unaudited private-only limit; this is a vendor claim, so verify.

items.name: Contabo API
items.why: VPS management API, e.g. reinstall an instance with a chosen image, SSH-key secrets and cloud-init user data; the cntb CLI wraps it.

items.name: WHOP checkout configurations API
items.why: Enables pay-what-you-want: the server creates a checkout with an inline plan at the buyer's chosen amount plus metadata. WHOP has no native PWYW or donation product.

investing-research.title: Investing research (free sites)
investing-research.description: Free investing and markets research sites: 13F and insider-trade trackers, investor letters, valuation data, macro sources, screeners and backtesters, with verdicts.

items.name: Dataroma
items.description: Free tracker of current portfolios and recent buys/sells of about 80 well-known value investors (superinvestors), built from 13F filings.
items.why: Fastest free way to see what famous investors hold. 13F data is up to 45 days old after each quarter and shows US long positions only.

items.name: WhaleWisdom
items.description: 13F filings database for hedge funds and institutions with quarterly changes, rankings and backtests; freemium.
items.why: Good depth, but most history, screeners and exports sit behind a paid plan. Dataroma and 13f.info cover the free basics.

items.name: Capitol Trades
items.description: Free tracker of stock trades disclosed by US members of Congress, searchable by politician, ticker and sector.
items.why: Popular content angle and easy to use. Disclosures can arrive up to 45 days after the trade, so treat it as context, not a trading signal.

items.name: OpenInsider
items.description: Free screener of SEC Form 4 insider trades: executives and directors buying or selling their own company's stock, with cluster-buy and large-purchase screens.
items.why: Insider buying clusters are a well-studied signal and the screens are free with no login. Data comes straight from SEC filings.

items.name: 13F Info
items.description: Searchable, readable view of SEC 13F filings by fund manager and by stock, including quarter-over-quarter changes.
items.why: Cleaner than reading raw EDGAR filings. Same 13F limits: quarterly, delayed, US long positions only.

items.name: Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters
items.description: Warren Buffett's annual letters to shareholders, free on Berkshire's own site, back to 1977.
items.why: Primary source on long-term investing and capital allocation; quote directly rather than from summaries.

items.name: Warren Buffett Archive (CNBC)
items.description: CNBC's archive of full Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting videos (31 meetings) with searchable transcripts.
items.why: Hours of primary-source Q&A. Fine for study and short quotes; the footage is CNBC's, so don't reuse clips in published videos.

items.name: Oaktree memos (Howard Marks)
items.description: Howard Marks' free client memos on market cycles, risk and investor psychology, archived back to 1990.
items.why: Some of the clearest writing on risk and cycles; free with no login.

items.name: Bridgewater research
items.description: Public research and macro essays from Ray Dalio's former firm Bridgewater Associates.
items.why: Only a slice is public; the Daily Observations remain client-only. Good for macro framing.

items.name: Principles (Ray Dalio)
items.description: Ray Dalio's site: free PDFs such as Big Debt Crises (email sign-up), the Principles in Action app and the PrinciplesYou assessment. The Principles book itself is paid.
items.why: The book is not free here, despite how lists describe the site. The free Big Debt Crises PDF is the most useful item.

items.name: GMO research (Jeremy Grantham)
items.description: GMO's research library, including Jeremy Grantham's quarterly letters and the 7-year asset class forecasts.
items.why: Long-horizon valuation view; some content needs a free registration.

items.name: AQR research
items.description: AQR Capital Management's papers, white papers and free factor datasets (value, momentum, quality) for backtesting.
items.why: Rigorous and free. The datasets are the practical part for anyone testing factor strategies.

items.name: Damodaran Online
items.description: NYU professor Aswath Damodaran's free valuation data (industry margins, betas, cost of capital, equity risk premiums, updated each January), spreadsheets and full course lectures.
items.why: The standard free source for valuation inputs. Download the spreadsheets rather than guessing discount rates.

items.name: Musings on Markets (Damodaran blog)
items.description: Aswath Damodaran's blog with worked valuations of companies in the news and annual data updates.
items.why: Shows the valuation method applied to real stocks, step by step.

items.name: Collaborative Fund blog
items.description: Essays on money behaviour and investing, historically by Morgan Housel (author of The Psychology of Money).
items.why: Excellent on investor psychology; not a data source.

items.name: Farnam Street
items.description: Shane Parrish's site on mental models and decision-making; many articles free, some members-only.
items.why: Useful frameworks for decisions; general, not market-specific.

items.name: J.P. Morgan Guide to the Markets
items.description: Quarterly free chart book from J.P. Morgan Asset Management covering valuations, earnings, rates, the economy and asset returns.
items.why: About 70 clean, sourced charts updated every quarter; great for education content (credit J.P. Morgan).

items.name: ARK Invest research
items.description: ARK Invest's research on disruptive innovation, including the annual Big Ideas report.
items.why: Interesting theses, but written by a fund that owns these stocks; its forecasts are often far too optimistic.

items.name: a16z
items.description: Andreessen Horowitz's essays and podcasts on startups, AI, crypto and tech trends.
items.why: Venture-capital view, written by investors in those companies; useful for tech trends, not for stock picking.

items.name: csinvesting.org
items.description: Former value-investing lecture-notes site. As of 2026-10 the domain shows an online poker review page.
items.why: Domain lapsed; the original content is gone. Don't link it.

items.name: Heilbrunn Center for Graham & Dodd Investing (Columbia)
items.description: Columbia Business School's value-investing centre: the free Value Investing with Legends podcast and the Graham & Doddsville student newsletter.
items.why: The old gsb.columbia.edu/valueinvesting address now redirects to the school homepage; use this one. Newsletter interviews with fund managers are the best part.

items.name: Federal Reserve
items.description: US central bank: FOMC statements, minutes, projections, speeches and data releases.
items.why: Primary source for rate decisions; FRED is easier for the data series.

items.name: European Central Bank
items.description: ECB monetary policy decisions, press conferences and the ECB Data Portal of euro-area statistics.
items.why: Primary source for euro-area rates and data.

items.name: Bank for International Settlements
items.description: The central banks' bank: annual and quarterly reviews, working papers and global statistics on credit, debt and FX.
items.why: Deep, free, slow-moving macro research; best for big-picture debt and liquidity topics.

items.name: Trading Economics
items.description: Economic indicators, calendars and forecasts for about 200 countries.
items.why: Free web view is handy for a quick look; downloads and the API are paid. Prefer FRED or the source agency for anything you publish.

items.name: Macrotrends
items.description: Free long-term charts of company financials, ratios and prices plus economic and commodity series, often 10 to 50+ years.
items.why: Quickest free way to see long-run history. Check key figures against filings before publishing.

items.name: Stock Analysis
items.description: Free company financials, statistics, ETF holdings, IPO calendar and screener for US and many global stocks; Pro plan adds longer history and exports.
items.why: The cleanest free financials site; the free tier is enough for most research.

items.name: CompaniesMarketCap
items.description: Rankings of the world's largest companies by market cap, revenue, earnings and more, by country and sector.
items.why: Fast for 'biggest companies' facts and content; not for analysis.

items.name: Finviz
items.description: Stock screener, market heat map, news and insider-trade view; free tier has delayed data, Elite is paid.
items.why: Free screener and heat map are excellent for daily market overviews.

items.name: Portfolio Visualizer
items.description: Portfolio backtesting, Monte Carlo, factor and asset-allocation analysis; core tools free, advanced ones paid.
items.why: Best free way to test an asset-allocation idea before committing money.

items.name: TradingView
items.description: Charting platform with indicators, Pine Script, screeners and community ideas; free tier with ads and limits, paid plans for more.
items.why: The default charting tool; the free tier covers most needs. Its data and charts are widely used in education content (follow their attribution rules).

items.name: Koyfin
items.description: Professional-style dashboards, charts, screeners and fundamentals; limited free tier, paid plans for full data.
items.why: Closest free-tier alternative to a Bloomberg-style terminal; test the free tier before paying.

items.name: AnnualReports.com
items.description: Archive of company annual reports in PDF form from many exchanges.
items.why: Convenient browsing, but use SEC EDGAR or the company's investor-relations site as the primary source.

items.name: Investor.gov
items.description: The SEC's free investor education site: calculators, fraud alerts and adviser background checks.
items.why: Trustworthy basics and the adviser lookup tool; good to cite in education content.

items.name: Bogleheads wiki
items.description: Community encyclopedia of passive, low-cost index investing, plus the Bogleheads forum.
items.why: Excellent on long-term index investing; US-centric for taxes and accounts.

items.name: Investopedia
items.description: Large free dictionary and explainer site for finance terms.
items.why: Fine for definitions; ad-heavy and not a primary source.

items.name: Corporate Finance Institute
items.description: Free guides and templates on financial modelling, valuation and accounting; certifications are paid.
items.why: Good free guides; the courses are an upsell.

items.name: CFA Institute Research Foundation
items.description: CFA Institute research publications and Research Foundation books, many free to download.
items.why: High-quality, often free monographs; some articles are member-only.

items.name: Morningstar
items.description: Fund and stock ratings, analyst research and portfolio tools; much of it now behind Morningstar Investor (paid).
items.why: Respected ratings, but the free tier is thin. Use it to look up fund ratings and fees.

items.name: Simply Wall St
items.description: Visual 'snowflake' company analysis and portfolio tracking; free plan limits the number of reports per month.
items.why: Good visuals, but the free plan is tight and the scores are model-driven; check the numbers yourself.

items.name: Value Investors Club
items.description: Members' detailed investment write-ups. Non-members see ideas 90 days late (45 days with an email sign-up); full access requires an application.
items.why: A great archive of how serious investors write a thesis; the delay makes it a learning resource, not a source of trades.

items.name: ETF Database
items.description: ETF screener, holdings lookup and category comparisons; some data paid.
items.why: Handy for 'what's inside this ETF'; the issuer's own site is the primary source.

items.name: Curvo
items.description: Dutch-regulated passive-investing app for Europeans; also offers a free backtest tool for European index funds at curvo.eu/backtest.
items.why: The backtester is useful for UCITS ETFs; the main site is now an investing app.

items.name: Of Dollars and Data
items.description: Nick Maggiulli's data-driven essays on investing and personal finance.
items.why: Clear, chart-based posts that test popular money claims with data.

items.name: A Wealth of Common Sense
items.description: Ben Carlson's blog on market history, long-term investing and behaviour.
items.why: Accessible market history with data; posts nearly daily.

items.name: The Irrelevant Investor
items.description: Michael Batnick's blog on markets and investor psychology; active as of 2026-10.
items.why: Short, timely takes on markets and behaviour.

items.name: Visual Capitalist
items.description: Infographics explaining markets, the economy and technology.
items.why: Great for ideas and context; graphics are copyrighted, so use them with permission or recreate them with the cited source data.
